title: The wrestling ground
hook: Guru Angad encourages exercise and wrestling so body and spirit grow strong together
tomorrow: an old man hears a hymn

segments.voice: Yesterday: kheer, Mata Khivi's rich rice pudding, served to everyone. The kitchen is a teacher.

There's an old idea, in a lot of places, that the spiritual life happens from the neck up. The body just carries your soul around, and maybe gets in the way. So holy people are pictured thin, pale and still. Khadur, in Guru Angad's day, looked different. In the mornings, hymns. At midday, the kitchen, with Mata Khivi's pudding. And in the evenings, tradition says, a patch of packed earth where young men stripped to the waist and wrestled, while the Guru himself watched and cheered them on.
screen: `SPIRITUAL FROM THE NECK UP?` → `KHADUR, IN GURU ANGAD'S DAY.` → `PACKED EARTH, AND WRESTLERS.`

segments.voice: That patch of earth is an akhara: a wrestling ground, a training place. Across South Asia, wrestling was an old and serious art, with its own teachers, its own discipline and its own pits of soft earth. Sikh tradition says Guru Angad set up an akhara at Khadur, and a gurdwara there is still named for it: the Mall Akhara, the wrestlers' ground. He encouraged young people to exercise, to wrestle, to be strong and healthy. Why would a Guru care about push-ups? Because on this path, the body isn't the enemy. Guru Nanak had told the yogis on the mountain that you don't need to leave the world to find God; you live in it, unstained. And living in the world takes a body that can work a field, carry water, stand up for a neighbor. Health isn't vanity; it's part of being useful. The picture shows up in the scripture too. In a hymn by the fifth Guru, Arjan, the speaker calls himself a wrestler, a champion of the Lord, come into the arena of the world. Life itself is the akhara, and Sikhs read the real opponents as inner ones, like ego, greed and anger. So the ground at Khadur was both things at once: a real place to train the body, and a picture of the struggle inside. Later Gurus would build on this, in harder times, but that story comes later.
screen: `AKHARA — A WRESTLING GROUND.` · `THE BODY ISN'T THE ENEMY.` · `STRONG ENOUGH TO BE USEFUL.` · `LIFE ITSELF IS THE ARENA.` · then, large: `THE BODY COUNTS TOO.`

segments.voice: For three minutes, stand if you can: roll your shoulders, stretch your arms up, fold forward, then march in place, do a few squats or walk around the room. If you can't stand, move what you can: hands, neck, breath. Don't make it a workout; make it a thank-you to the body that carries you.
Akhara. A wrestling ground; at Khadur, a place where Guru Angad had young people train their bodies alongside their spirits. Today's word.
Your line: the body counts too. Tomorrow, an old man hears a hymn. Nice work today.

howItsDone: Sikh tradition values physical health and strength alongside prayer; gurdwaras sometimes host sports, and martial arts such as gatka are practiced in Sikh communities, with Khadur Sahib's Mall Akhara remembered as Guru Angad's wrestling ground.
